::: {.why}
At a signal-to-noise ratio this low, variance reduction is worth more than bias reduction, which reverses the usual ordering of these two model families and is worth being able to argue.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Say why averaging many high-variance models is particularly effective at low signal-to-noise, and check it on your data.
- Implement bagging with the sample size set by label uniqueness rather than by the row count.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>65 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Make the argument quantitative: plot out-of-sample R-squared against the number of trees for both a forest and a boosting ensemble, and report where each saturates. Then compare the variance of predictions across bootstrap-refits for each model family.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Fix the bagging that is wrong by default: standard bootstrap sampling draws as many rows as exist, which massively oversamples given your effective sample size from day 213. Refit with the sample size set to the effective count and report the difference. This is a correction almost nobody makes and it usually helps.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Note the ensemble that costs nothing: averaging the linear and boosting predictions often beats both, and it is worth measuring before you conclude anything about which family wins.
:::
:::
